questions.title: Attribute types
questions.prompt: Select the attribute types for rank, title, budget, and average rating.
questions.answer: Rank is ordinal (ordered positions without meaningful arithmetic). Title is categorical (names). Budget is quantitative (amount of money). Average rating is quantitative when it is a numerical average; although individual star ratings may be ordinal, the question says average rating.
questions.note: These are four separate classifications. The original paper rearranges the choices in different versions.

questions.title: Scatterplot matrices and parallel coordinates
questions.prompt: State FOUR tasks or findings that a scatterplot matrix can support. State ONE task better supported by parallel coordinates.
questions.answer: A scatterplot matrix lets users compare pairwise relationships for many variables, identify positive or negative correlations, find clusters of similar records, and spot unusual observations or outliers across pairs. Parallel coordinates can be especially useful for tracing how an individual multidimensional record behaves across several ordered attributes, or for comparing patterns across many attributes in one continuous path. Both can show multivariate data, but each has different tradeoffs in clutter and interpretation.
questions.note: The question asks for four distinct matrix uses and one separate parallel-coordinate advantage.

questions.title: Star plots and parallel coordinates
questions.prompt: State two layout similarities, one layout difference, one advantage of a star plot, and one advantage of parallel coordinates.
questions.answer: Both place several variables on separate axes and represent each item using values connected across those axes. Both enable comparisons of multivariate profiles, and their axis order can affect how patterns appear. A star plot uses axes radiating from a common center; parallel coordinates use parallel (usually vertical) axes connected by a polyline. A star plot can provide a compact shape or profile for a single record, helpful for comparing several small glyphs. Parallel coordinates make it easier to inspect many records at once and brush ranges across multiple dimensions, though overplotting becomes a problem.
questions.note: The source has an inconsistent sentence mentioning Parallel Sets even though its heading and questions refer to Parallel Coordinates. The intended term is not silently changed; see original paper.

questions.title: Visual channels
questions.prompt: Order {Length, Position on unaligned scale, Volume, Color saturation, Area} by effectiveness for a continuous attribute. Explain visual popout and name three channels that can produce it.
questions.answer: For these five channels, effectiveness from strongest to weakest is position on an unaligned scale, length, area, color saturation, volume. Popout occurs when one item is noticed almost immediately, before a deliberate item-by-item search, because it differs clearly from its neighbours. Examples of cues that can produce popout include contrasting color hue, distinctive orientation, and motion. Whether something pops out depends on the display and competing items; it is not guaranteed for every difference.
questions.note: Visual encoding lecture includes an effectiveness ranking and the concepts of accuracy, discriminability, and popout.

questions.title: Scalability of time-oriented visualizations
questions.prompt: Give one suitable technique for 5, 20 and 100 time series. Do not use line, bar or scatter plots, and do not repeat a technique.
questions.answer: Possible defensible combination: 5 series: braided graph (relationships are visible if clutter remains manageable); 20 series: small multiples (separate the series while keeping a shared scale for comparison); 100 series: horizon graphs (compress each time series into narrow strips) or a heatmap if suitable. Explain the tradeoff: overlaid plots get cluttered as series increase, small multiples use screen space, and compact displays sacrifice some detail. These are reasoned sample choices, not an official answer key; several combinations may be accepted if justified.
questions.note: No official marking guide was supplied. Multiple defensible chart assignments exist.

questions.title: Tree visualizations and parent-child relations
questions.prompt: Match Sunburst diagram, Node-Link diagrams and Treemaps with Adjacency, Containment and Line.
questions.answer: Sunburst diagram → Adjacency, where parent and child levels are adjacent radial rings; Node-link diagram → Line, since explicit edges connect nodes; Treemap → Containment, as children are rectangles nested within parents.
questions.note: This is a mapping task, and the option order differs between the files.

questions.title: Trees and tasks
questions.prompt: Match Icicle layout, Treemaps and Node-Link diagrams with spotting outliers in leaf nodes, following paths, and summing values of children.
questions.answer: Icicle layout → spotting outliers among leaf nodes (compare the sizes/shapes of leaf segments); Treemaps → summing values of children (area aggregates up into parents); Node-link diagrams → following paths (visible connections through the tree). The exact advantage can depend on layout and encoding.
questions.note: The original form orders the rows and tasks differently across versions.

questions.title: Daily temperature visualizations
questions.prompt: For maximum daily temperature across one year in ten cities, give advantages and disadvantages of line graph with grid, braided graph, stacked area chart, small multiples, and horizon graphs.
questions.answer: Line chart with grid: time trends and exact values are relatively easy to inspect, but ten overlapping lines can clutter the view. Braided graph: crossing and ordering changes can be emphasized; overlaps can obscure individual values and make tracing lines hard. Stacked area chart: conveys the total and group contributions, but individual cities away from the baseline are hard to compare accurately; temperature is not always meaningful to sum. Small multiples: gives each city its own uncluttered view and supports comparison with shared scales, but costs display space and makes exact cross-panel comparisons slower. Horizon graphs: compress many series for a compact overview and reveal patterns, but have a learning cost, require a clear reference/baseline, and hide fine details.
questions.note: The question is asking for pros AND cons for all five types; a single generic paragraph is insufficient.

questions.title: Identify the InfoVis technique
questions.prompt: Identify the technique in the image showing a large time-series detail and a smaller interactive overview. Choose Semantic Zooming, Overview+Detail, Focus and Context, or Detail on Demand.
questions.answer: Overview+Detail. The figure displays both a detailed time-series window and a separate miniature overview with a highlighted range indicating the detailed selection. Neither view simply replaces the other.
questions.note: The image on original page 5 is part of the question.

questions.title: Pattern matching
questions.prompt: Match the scatterplots and parallel-coordinate plots that represent the same data. Use the diagrams from the original exam page 6.
questions.answer: Compare the ordering and relative patterns of records across axes: a pairwise scatterplot’s two coordinate variables should correspond to the same axes in parallel coordinates. Match strong positive trends to mostly parallel crossing behaviour, negative trends to more crossing between axes, and clusters/outliers consistently. Because the question is diagram-specific and no official matching key was provided, compare your work to the original image rather than treating a guessed mapping as certain.
questions.note: Requires the figure on page 6 and self-review; no verified official mapping supplied.

questions.title: Graph visualization
questions.prompt: Which visualization techniques are suitable for general graphs? Consider enclosure, node-link diagrams, adjacency diagrams, and adjacency matrices.
questions.answer: Node-link diagrams and adjacency matrices are standard representations of general graphs. Arc/adjacency diagrams can also show connections among graph vertices using links. Enclosure layouts are most directly suited to nested hierarchies (trees), so they are not a generally applicable representation for arbitrary graph edges. The distinction is whether the technique can encode general relationships, not only parent–child containment.
questions.note: The source displays a marking grid rather than a clear text-only answer key.

questions.title: Tree visualization
questions.prompt: Which of adjacency matrix, enclosure, adjacency diagrams and node-link diagrams are suitable for trees?
questions.answer: A tree is a special kind of graph. Node-link diagrams show parent–child links clearly, while enclosure techniques such as treemaps show a nested hierarchy through containment. An adjacency matrix can represent the links of a tree, although it is not usually the most efficient way to trace ancestry. Adjacency diagrams can also show tree edges, depending on the form of the diagram. Distinguish “can represent” from “well-suited for typical hierarchy tasks”; the original question may assess appropriateness.
questions.note: Original marking-grid options need the original page to interpret fully.

questions.title: Observable Plot 1
questions.prompt: Recreate the chart using Observable Plot and dataset nyData: x=date, y=medianAskingPrice, color by neighborhood and circle radius mapped to priceCutShare.
questions.answer: Example pattern, to adapt to the supplied dataset and chart: Plot.plot({marks:[Plot.dot(nyData,{x:"date",y:"medianAskingPrice",stroke:"neighborhood",r:"priceCutShare"})]});. Note that the source plot uses hollow circles, making stroke a more faithful color encoding than fill. The complete working result depends on Observable Plot version and the data values.
questions.note: This is a practice solution, not official instructor code. See the source image on page 7.

questions.title: Observable Plot 2
questions.prompt: Using dataset worldbank, recreate x=income_group, y=life_exp, color by income_group, facet by region; add legend, correct colors/order and appropriate y-axis range.
questions.answer: Possible Observable Plot structure: Plot.plot({color:{domain:["Low income","Lower middle income","Upper middle income","High income"],range:["red","orange","green","blue"],legend:true},x:{domain:["Low income","Lower middle income","Upper middle income","High income"]},y:{domain:[54,86]},fx:{label:"region"},marks:[Plot.dot(worldbank,{x:"income_group",y:"life_exp",stroke:"income_group",fx:"region"})]});. Adjust margins and axes to match the paper. The screenshot uses hollow circles, so stroke is more appropriate than fill. Check your code in the course’s Observable Plot environment.
questions.note: Source figure shows red, orange, green, blue categories and y ticks approximately 54–86.

questions.answer: Line chart with grid: time trends and exact values are relatively easy to inspect, but ten overlapping lines can clutter the view. Braided graph: crossing and ordering changes can be emphasized; overlaps can obscure individual values and make tracing lines hard. Stacked area chart: conveys the total and group contributions, but individual cities away from the baseline are hard to compare accurately; temperature is not always meaningful to sum. Small multiples: gives each city its own uncluttered view and supports comparison with shared scales, but costs display space and makes exact cross-panel comparisons slower. Horizon graphs: compress many series for a compact overview and reveal patterns, but have a learning cost, require a clear reference/baseline, and hide fine details.
questions.note: The question is asking for pros AND cons for all five types; a single generic paragraph is insufficient.

questions.title: Graph visualization
questions.prompt: Which visualization techniques are suitable for general graphs? Consider enclosure, node-link diagrams, adjacency diagrams, and adjacency matrices.
questions.answer: Node-link diagrams and adjacency matrices are standard representations of general graphs. Arc/adjacency diagrams can also show connections among graph vertices using links. Enclosure layouts are most directly suited to nested hierarchies (trees), so they are not a generally applicable representation for arbitrary graph edges. The distinction is whether the technique can encode general relationships, not only parent–child containment.

questions.title: Tree visualization
questions.prompt: Which of adjacency matrix, enclosure, adjacency diagrams and node-link diagrams are suitable for trees?
questions.answer: A tree is a special kind of graph. Node-link diagrams show parent–child links clearly, while enclosure techniques such as treemaps show a nested hierarchy through containment. An adjacency matrix can represent the links of a tree, although it is not usually the most efficient way to trace ancestry. Adjacency diagrams can also show tree edges, depending on the form of the diagram. Distinguish “can represent” from “well-suited for typical hierarchy tasks”; the original question may assess appropriateness.
questions.note: Original marking-grid options need the original page to interpret fully.

questions.title: Observable Plot 1
questions.prompt: Recreate the chart using Observable Plot and dataset nyData: x=date, y=medianAskingPrice, color by neighborhood and circle radius mapped to priceCutShare.
questions.answer: Example pattern, to adapt to the supplied dataset and chart: Plot.plot({marks:[Plot.dot(nyData,{x:"date",y:"medianAskingPrice",stroke:"neighborhood",r:"priceCutShare"})]});. Note that the source plot uses hollow circles, making stroke a more faithful color encoding than fill. The complete working result depends on Observable Plot version and the data values.
questions.note: This is a practice solution, not official instructor code. See the source image on page 7.

questions.title: Observable Plot 2
questions.prompt: Using dataset worldbank, recreate x=income_group, y=life_exp, color by income_group, facet by region; add legend, correct colors/order and appropriate y-axis range.
